pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Endangered & Extinct Species (ages 9–11): why species become endangered (at risk of extinction) or go extinct (gone forever) — habitat destruction, hunting/poaching, pollution, climate change, invasive species — and that scientists track threat levels using the IUCN Red List.
• Standards — UK (DfE): links Y4 'environments can change and pose dangers to living things' and Y6 adaptation/evolution to human-driven and natural threats; supports the wider science-and-society aims.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS4-4 (make a claim about [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-LS4-4]); MS-LS2-4 (changes to an ecosystem affect populations); connects to human impacts.
• Operational details: define endangered (high risk of extinction) vs extinct (no individuals remain) precisely. Cover the main causes with examples — habitat loss (orangutan, deforestation), poaching/hunting (rhino, elephant ivory), pollution, climate change (polar bear, coral), invasive species (many island birds). Use flagship examples: giant panda, mountain gorilla, Amur leopard (endangered); dodo, thylacine (extinct). Introduce the IUCN Red List as the standard categories (Least Concern → Vulnerable → Endangered → Critically Endangered → Extinct in the Wild → Extinct) scientists use to classify risk from evidence.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~9): define endangered vs extinct and name examples of each. B (transitional, ~10): name at least 3 causes of endangerment with an example each. C (formal, ~11): explain that the IUCN Red List ranks species by extinction risk from evidence, and reason about which cause threatens a given species.
bestPractices: Fix the endangered–extinct distinction first with unambiguous examples (panda = endangered, still alive; dodo = extinct, none left) before discussing causes.
Treat causes as an evidence-based diagnosis — given a species, which threats apply? — rather than a list to memorise, so pupils reason about specific situations.
Introduce the IUCN Red List as a scientific ranking from data (population size, range, decline rate), modelling how experts turn evidence into a category rather than opinion.
Keep it honest but not hopeless — pair threats with the fact that categories can improve, setting up the conservation topic without despair.
keyRepresentations: The IUCN Red List category ladder (Least Concern → … → Extinct) with example species placed on it.
A cause–species matching board (habitat loss, poaching, pollution, climate change, invasives).
A population-decline graph showing a species dropping toward the endangered/extinct threshold.
A before/after habitat pair illustrating habitat destruction as a cause.
commonMisconceptions: 'Endangered and extinct mean the same thing' — endangered = at high risk but still alive; extinct = none remain.
'Extinction is always caused by humans' — extinction also occurs naturally, though current rates are greatly raised by human activity.
'Extinct animals can be brought back easily' — extinction is (currently) permanent; there is no simple undo.
'If a few individuals survive, the species is safe' — very small populations can still be doomed (low genetic diversity, unable to recover).
'The Red List is just an opinion / a list of favourites' — it is an evidence-based scientific classification of extinction risk.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11 (Endangered & Extinct Species): establish precisely that endangered means a species is at high risk but still surviving, while extinct means none remain anywhere. Pupils diagnose WHY specific species decline — habitat destruction (usually the leading driver), hunting/poaching, pollution, climate change, invasive species — using evidence (population trend, range, threats) rather than memorising a list, and learn the IUCN Red List as an evidence-based scientific ranking of extinction risk, not an opinion.

activities.title: Species case-file: become a Red List assessor
feedback: If a pupil places a thriving species as endangered or vice versa, point back to the evidence: is the population trend declining and how steeply, how many animals remain, and how small is its range?
If a pupil treats the category as opinion, show that the real classification follows stated criteria (population size, range, decline rate) and ask which criterion their species meets.

A species a pupil thinks of as 'endangered' in the everyday sense may currently sit at a different rung — for example the giant panda is presently classed as Vulnerable, not in the Endangered category. Use this to reinforce that the actual category is an evidence-based judgement that can differ from a familiar label.
Praise justifications that cite specific evidence ('its range shrank and numbers fell by half') over bare category names.
activities.rationale: Classifying from evidence models how experts turn data into a category, directly countering the misconception that the Red List is 'just an opinion'. Diagnosing per species treats causes as reasoning rather than rote recall.
sourceClaims: The IUCN Red List classifies species into risk categories (Least Concern, Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered, Extinct in the Wild, Extinct) based on evidence such as population size, range, and rate of decline.
learnerActions: Open a 'file' for a real species (e.g. giant panda, mountain gorilla, Amur leopard) containing a population graph over time, the size of its range, and the threats it faces.

Decide where the species belongs on the risk ladder (Least Concern → Near Threatened → Vulnerable → Endangered → Critically Endangered → Extinct in the Wild → Extinct) and justify the placement from the evidence shown.
Compare your placement with the species' actual, current Red List classification and state what evidence drove the real decision.

For each species, write one sentence naming the main threat and how it drives the decline (e.g. 'deforestation removes the orangutan's food and shelter, so its numbers can fall even without any hunting').
activities.intendedInsight: Endangered and extinct are different points on one evidence-based scale, and a species' position is a measured judgement from population size, range and rate of decline — not a label or a favourite.

activities.title: Live pressure: watch a species slide down the ladder
feedback: If a pupil expects an instant jump to extinct, highlight that the curve bends gradually and crosses thresholds in stages.
If a pupil thinks only hunting matters, have them run the habitat-loss slider with poaching set to zero and watch the population still crash.
Note explicitly that a small surviving population is not automatically safe — very low numbers can still decline toward extinction.
activities.rationale: A controllable pressure that visibly moves the population curve makes the cause–effect link concrete and addresses the misconception that a few survivors mean safety. This is an optional interactive mechanism, offered to make the mechanism visible, not a required format.
sourceClaims: Changes to an ecosystem affect populations; solutions can be proposed when the environment changes.

Major drivers of endangerment/extinction are habitat destruction, overexploitation (hunting/poaching), pollution, climate change, and invasive species; current extinction rates are far above natural background rates.
learnerActions: Starting from a stable population, increase a single pressure (e.g. habitat loss, or poaching) a little at a time.
Watch the population curve bend downward and note at what point the species crosses from one risk category into the next.
Describe in words what happened: which pressure you changed, and how far along the ladder it pushed the species.
Repeat with a different pressure to compare how different threats drive decline.
activities.intendedInsight: Specific human pressures push a species along the risk scale; 'endangered' becomes a measured position driven by evidence, and conservation can be pictured as pushing species back up the ladder.

activities.title: Cause diagnosis: why is THIS animal at risk?
feedback: If a pupil names only hunting, trace how clearing a forest removes food and shelter so a population declines with no hunting at all.
If a pupil uses 'endangered' and 'extinct' interchangeably, re-anchor with panda (at risk, still alive) versus dodo (extinct, none remain).

If a pupil remembers from the case-file that the panda's current IUCN category is Vulnerable, affirm both are true: in this broad endangered-vs-extinct sort it counts as 'at risk but still alive', while on the strict IUCN ladder its current evidence-based rung is Vulnerable.
Confirm that extinction is currently permanent, and that captive breeding alone cannot rebuild a wild population once the habitat it needs has been lost — rather than implying breeding never works.
activities.rationale: Explicit sorting fixes the endangered/extinct distinction with unambiguous flagship examples, and diagnosing indirect causes targets the dominant misconception that only hunting endangers species.
sourceClaims: Major drivers of endangerment/extinction are habitat destruction, overexploitation (hunting/poaching), pollution, climate change, and invasive species; current extinction rates are far above natural background rates.
learnerActions: For several declining species, match each to the threat(s) actually driving its decline (habitat loss → orangutan/deforestation; poaching → rhino horn/elephant ivory; climate change → polar bear/coral; invasive species → island birds; pollution → species harmed by chemicals or plastics in their habitat).
For at least one species, explain how an indirect cause (habitat loss) harms the animal even when no one is hunting it — what food, shelter or breeding space is lost.
Sort example species into 'endangered (still alive, at risk)' versus 'extinct (none left)', placing panda and mountain gorilla as endangered and dodo and thylacine as extinct.
activities.intendedInsight: Different animals are endangered for different, identifiable reasons; habitat destruction is usually the leading driver even without direct killing; and endangered is firmly distinct from extinct.

activities.title: Shrinking-habitat investigation (physical, no screen needed)
feedback: Draw out that the crash happened purely from lost space, directly challenging the 'only hunting matters' idea.
Use the spoken prompts to surface whether pupils still conflate endangered with extinct or think extinction is reversible, and reteach as needed.
Keep the tone honest but not hopeless: note that categories can improve, setting up conservation without despair.
activities.rationale: A kinaesthetic model of habitat loss lets pupils feel the population crash from space alone, and the discussion prompts double as diagnostic probes. Serves as a no-technology alternative that builds the same causal reasoning.
sourceClaims: Environments can change and this can pose dangers to living things; adaptation and evolution frame why change threatens species.
Changes to an ecosystem affect populations; solutions can be proposed when the environment changes.
learnerActions: Mark out a large area as a 'habitat' and have pupils stand as 'animals', each needing personal space to survive.
Predict how many animals can survive, then repeatedly halve the habitat area and record how many must leave each time.
Discuss: no one was 'hunting' — so why did the population crash? Connect this to real deforestation, wetland draining and reef damage.

Respond to prompts: Could a rainforest monkey become endangered if no one hunted it? What is the difference between endangered and extinct? Why can't we always bring an extinct animal back? What is the IUCN Red List for?
activities.intendedInsight: Habitat loss alone, with no hunting, can drive a species toward extinction — making the leading, indirect cause tangible.

activities.title: In role: how an assessor decides a category (optional hook)
feedback: If pupils only repeat the explanation back, ask them to point to the specific evidence in a species file that would change the category.

Reinforce that the explanation is a starting hook; the real skill is doing the diagnosis from evidence. A role-play explanation can introduce the criteria but does not by itself show a pupil can classify a new species.
activities.rationale: An expert-in-role explanation can introduce how categories are decided, but diagnosing from evidence remains the core skill, so this is framed as an optional lead-in rather than the main activity.
sourceClaims: The IUCN Red List classifies species into risk categories (Least Concern, Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered, Extinct in the Wild, Extinct) based on evidence such as population size, range, and rate of decline.
learnerActions: Read or listen to a short explanation, in the voice of a conservation scientist, of how a Red List category is chosen from evidence.
Note which pieces of evidence the assessor says they weigh (population size, range, rate of decline).
Then return to a case-file and apply the same reasoning to justify a category yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: Red List categories come from stated evidence and criteria, so classification is reasoned, not arbitrary.

constraints: Fix the endangered–extinct distinction first with unambiguous examples (panda = at risk, still alive; dodo = extinct, none left) before discussing causes.
Teach causes as an evidence-based diagnosis of specific species, not a list to memorise.
Present the IUCN Red List as a scientific classification from data (population size, range, decline rate), not an opinion or a list of favourites.

Distinguish the everyday 'endangered = at risk, alive' sense from the specific IUCN 'Endangered' category; in ladder/case-file tasks use each species' real current category (e.g. the giant panda is presently Vulnerable) as the evidence-based answer.

Be honest that extinction is currently permanent; captive breeding alone cannot restore a wild population once the habitat it needs has been lost. Do not imply extinct animals can be easily brought back, nor that captive breeding never works where habitat remains.

Note that extinction also occurs naturally over long timescales, but current rates are greatly raised by rapid human-driven change that outpaces a species' ability to adapt — avoid 'it's the animal's own fault' framing.
A very small surviving population is not automatically safe; low numbers can still decline toward extinction.

Sorting/matching and ladder-ordering tasks check whether pupils can classify and catch the endangered/extinct conflation, but recognising a correct match does not by itself show pupils can independently diagnose a new species from its evidence — pair them with explanation tasks.

Ensure all five named causes (habitat loss, hunting/poaching, pollution, climate change, invasive species) appear somewhere in the diagnosis activities; pollution has no single flagship species in the sources, so keep its example generic rather than inventing one.
The live-pressure slider and physical habitat model are illustrative approximations of population dynamics; real declines depend on many interacting factors.
Keep the tone honest but not hopeless: pair threats with the fact that categories can improve, setting up conservation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; all sources[].claim were marked verified:false in the row and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source states habitat destruction is 'usually the leading driver' and the diagnostic treats this as the discriminating answer. This is broadly supported for many terrestrial species but the single 'biggest cause' varies by taxon and region (e.g. overexploitation dominates for many marine and large-vertebrate species); the activities present it as 'usually leading' rather than universally dominant. Reviewers may wish to confirm the claim's scope for the specific examples used.

The claim that 'current extinction rates are far above natural background rates' is cited to a generic 'conservation-biology reference' with verified:false; retain but verify the source before presenting as settled fact to pupils.

The original row labels the giant panda as 'endangered'. This is accurate in the broad 'at risk but alive' sense, but the panda's current IUCN category is Vulnerable (reclassified 2016). When species are placed on the strict IUCN ladder, treat the real current category as the evidence-based answer rather than assuming 'Endangered'; verify each flagship species' current category (e.g. Amur leopard Critically Endangered, mountain gorilla Endangered) before use.

assess.poeTask: Mark out a large 'habitat' and have students ('animals') each need a personal space to stand. Ask them to predict how many can survive as you repeatedly halve the habitat area. The population crashes as the space shrinks — showing that habitat loss alone, with no hunting at all, can drive a species toward extinction.
probeDeeper: If no one hunted a rainforest monkey at all, could it still become endangered? How?
What's the difference between a species that's endangered and one that's extinct?
Why can't we always just bring an extinct animal back?
What is the IUCN Red List for, and how do scientists use it?
assess.correctAnswer: Hunting and poaching matter, but for most species the biggest cause is habitat destruction — when forests are cleared, wetlands drained or reefs damaged, animals lose the places they need to feed, shelter and breed, so whole populations decline even when no one hunts them. Pollution, climate change and invasive species add to this. So the main driver is usually loss of habitat, not shooting.

errorPatterns.pattern: Animals only become endangered because people hunt or kill them directly
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce habitat destruction as the leading cause; trace how clearing a forest removes food and shelter even when no one hunts the animals.
errorPatterns.distractor: The main cause is hunters shooting too many animals.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists only hunting or poaching; overlooks habitat destruction.

errorPatterns.pattern: Extinction isn't a real problem — if numbers drop we can just breed more, or the animals will come back
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that extinction is permanent — gone forever — and that once habitat is lost, breeding alone can't restore a wild population.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats extinction as recoverable or assumes captive breeding always fixes it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Species go extinct because they were weak or failed to adapt — it's just natural and their own fault
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish slow natural background extinction from today's rapid, human-driven change that outpaces a species' ability to adapt.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the animal 'couldn't keep up', with no mention of rapid human-caused change.

errorPatterns.pattern: Endangered and extinct mean the same thing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Endangered means at high risk but still surviving; extinct means none left anywhere — the Red List ranks these stages.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks extinction is caused only by direct hunting, or that it's reversible and natural and doesn't matter; confuses endangered with extinct.
responseLevels.full: Defines endangered versus extinct, identifies habitat destruction as the leading cause while naming others (hunting, pollution, climate change, invasive species), explains how indirect causes drive decline, understands extinction is permanent, and knows the IUCN Red List tracks a species' level of risk.
responseLevels.partial: Names several causes and examples and knows the Red List exists, but treats the causes as an unranked list — can't say habitat destruction is usually the leading driver, or explain how an indirect cause pushes a species down without anyone hunting it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: More species are becoming endangered today than ever before. A student says the main reason is that hunters are shooting too many animals. Is hunting really the biggest cause — or is something else driving most species toward extinction?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who pictures extinction only as direct killing names hunting and stops. A child who understands names habitat destruction (and other systemic causes) as the leading driver and explains why losing a place harms a species. Identifying the dominant, indirect cause is the discriminator.
